interview_metadata.name: Judith Castillo
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Atlanta and grew up mostly in Gwinnett County, around Lilburn and Tucker. My parents were very middle-class, very education-focused people. My dad's side has Hispanic roots, and my mom's family is mostly European ancestry, so our house had this mix of Southern routines, big holiday meals, Braves games, and a lot of extended-family stories about working hard and staying grounded. I was a careful kid, honestly. I liked puzzles, library books, organizing things, and I was the person in group projects who made the spreadsheet before anyone asked for one. In high school I was strong in math and business classes, but I also loved choir concerts, festivals, and being around the different cultures in Gwinnett. I went to the University of Georgia for finance, then later earned an MBA while working. That period shaped me because I learned I did not just like numbers; I liked translating numbers for people who were making decisions. Career-wise, I started as a financial analyst, moved into budgeting and forecasting, learned Excel modeling, VBA, SAP, NetSuite, Power BI, and Tableau, and gradually became a financial manager. I have never been married and I do not have children, but I have close family nearby and a strong circle through work, yoga, Toastmasters, running, cooking meetups, and volunteering. The big thread in my life is trying to be both disciplined and open: disciplined with money, career goals, and health, but open to travel, food, music, mentoring younger analysts, and being part of the community.

follow_ups.question: When you think about childhood in Gwinnett County, what concrete memories stand out?
follow_ups.response: Saturday errands with my mom on Lawrenceville Highway, school festivals where every table had different food, and my dad keeping a Braves game on the radio while he worked in the garage. I remember feeling like the world was bigger than our subdivision.

follow_ups.question: Who were you closest to growing up?
follow_ups.response: My younger brother Daniel and my mom. Daniel and I fought like siblings, but we were close, and my mom was the person who noticed when I was overwhelmed before I would say anything.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The clearest crossroads was after my first analyst job. I had an offer to move into a narrower accounting role that would have been stable and predictable, and at the same time my company was starting a finance transformation project. The project was messier: new ERP workflows, reporting issues, senior leaders asking questions no one had clean answers for. I decided to stay with the project because I wanted to be closer to strategy, not just close the books. I spent nights teaching myself VBA and later Power BI, and I volunteered to present a dashboard to operations leaders. That choice changed my reputation. People stopped seeing me as just the person who produced the numbers and started seeing me as someone who could connect finance, operations, and technology. It made my current career path possible.

follow_ups.question: What made that project feel risky at the time?
follow_ups.response: There was no neat playbook. If the dashboards were wrong or the data mapping failed, everyone saw it, including senior leadership.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone encourage you to take that path?
follow_ups.response: A former manager named Carla did. She told me, 'You explain complicated things without making people feel stupid,' and that stuck with me.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I made a pros and cons list, talked with Carla, and decided that growth mattered more than comfort at that point.

follow_ups.question: How long did you think about it?
follow_ups.response: Probably two weeks seriously, with a lot of Sunday-evening overthinking.

follow_ups.question: What was the deciding factor?
follow_ups.response: I realized I would regret not learning the technology side more than I would regret a stressful year.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. A formal mentoring program or training budget would have helped. I pieced together a lot through YouTube, internal manuals, and trial and error.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Protected time to learn and a senior sponsor who could help me navigate the politics of the project.

follow_ups.question: Did you later offer that kind of help to others?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I now build learning plans for junior analysts instead of just throwing them into reporting cycles.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am not married, I am not living with a partner, and I do not have children. My parents still live within driving distance, and I see them usually twice a month, more around birthdays and holidays. My younger brother Daniel lives in Decatur with his wife, and I am close to them; we do dinners, Braves games, and the occasional hike when we can coordinate schedules. My family is supportive but not intrusive, which I appreciate. They know I am career-focused, but they also remind me not to turn every part of life into a five-year plan. I have cousins around metro Atlanta too, though I see them mostly at family events. Family for me is not a huge daily household situation, but it is a steady emotional anchor.

follow_ups.question: What do family gatherings usually look like?
follow_ups.response: Food-heavy and loud in a good way. My mom makes roast chicken or tamales depending on the occasion, I bring sourdough or a curry, and someone has sports on.

follow_ups.question: Do they influence your major decisions?
follow_ups.response: I ask their opinions, but I make my own decisions. My parents are practical, so they usually ask about savings, commute, and whether I am sleeping enough.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My sister-in-law Maya is part of my immediate circle now. We text about recipes and sometimes meet for coffee in Decatur.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk with her?
follow_ups.response: A couple of times a week by text, usually light things.

follow_ups.question: Does she join family events?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she is fully part of those dinners and holiday plans.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are a small group from different parts of life. Priya is a friend from my MBA program, and we do monthly cooking meetups. Lauren is from Atlanta Running Club, and we sign up for charity 5Ks together. I also have a work friend, Marcus, who is another finance manager and a good sounding board. I date occasionally, mostly through friends or apps, but I am not in a committed relationship right now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your friends in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually once or twice a week, depending on work. Sunday yoga or a weeknight dinner is common.

follow_ups.question: What do you rely on them for?
follow_ups.response: Perspective. They help me get out of my own head when I am too focused on work.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Lilburn, Georgia, in the 30047 area, in a townhouse community that is quiet but not isolated. I like that I can get to groceries, parks, and small restaurants quickly, and I am close enough to Atlanta for work events, concerts, and theatre without living in the middle of the city. The neighborhood has families, retirees, and young professionals, and people wave or chat by the mailboxes. Gwinnett is very diverse, and I love that I can get good Korean food, tacos, Thai groceries, and Southern barbecue within a short drive. Traffic can be frustrating, but the area feels practical and rooted.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often nearby?
follow_ups.response: Lilburn City Park, the farmers market when it is running, Publix, H Mart, and a couple of local coffee shops.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few. I know Angela next door well enough to exchange garden vegetables and watch for packages.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I generally feel safe. I am aware of my surroundings when running early or coming home late, but I do not feel afraid in my neighborhood.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you feel less comfortable?
follow_ups.response: Late at night in poorly lit parking lots, mostly. That is more general caution than specific fear.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we have a community text thread for packages, cars, and maintenance issues.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The ups are diversity, affordability compared with central Atlanta, and being near family. The downs are traffic, occasional sprawl, and having to drive for almost everything.

follow_ups.question: What would you change if you could?
follow_ups.response: More walkable streets and better transit connections into Atlanta.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Community, family proximity, and the fact that my routines are built here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live alone in my townhouse. No partner, children, roommates, or relatives live with me. I like having a quiet place after work because my job involves a lot of meetings and decision-making. My home is organized but lived-in: kitchen equipment, books, plants, a small vegetable garden outside, and usually a puzzle on the coffee table.

follow_ups.question: Do you prefer living alone?
follow_ups.response: At this stage, yes. I like hosting people, but I also need quiet to reset.

follow_ups.question: Who visits most often?
follow_ups.response: My brother and sister-in-law, a couple of close friends, and sometimes my parents for Sunday lunch.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me permanently.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone stayed recently?
follow_ups.response: No one recently for more than a night.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not currently.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Occasionally a friend might stay after a late concert in Atlanta, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: How often is rare?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three times a year.

follow_ups.question: Any family overnight visits?
follow_ups.response: Not usually, since they live close enough to drive home.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. No one else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: Any college students tied to the household?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Anyone away for medical care?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I usually start around 6:15 with coffee, a quick budget or news check, and either yoga, a short run, or stretching. I work roughly 8:30 to 6:00, with heavier days during forecast cycles and month-end. Two or three days a week I work from home, and the rest I go into the office or visit project teams. Evenings vary: Toastmasters twice a month, cooking meetup once a month, yoga class at Lilburn Yoga Collective, or dinner with friends. Weekends are for hiking, errands, meal prep, volunteering with financial-literacy workshops, and sometimes live music or a Braves game.

follow_ups.question: What is your busiest day?
follow_ups.response: Usually Tuesday, because leadership meetings tend to stack up and I am often reviewing dashboards by late afternoon.

follow_ups.question: What does a calmer day look like?
follow_ups.response: A work-from-home Friday with focused modeling work, lunch at home, and an evening walk before cooking.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work full time as a financial manager for a mid-sized company in the Atlanta metro area. My work is budgeting, forecasting, financial reporting, risk review, and leading finance transformation projects. I manage analysts, review models, build executive dashboards, and translate financial data into decisions for operations and senior leadership. My normal hours are business hours, but finance has seasons: month-end, budget planning, audits, and board reporting can push me into evenings.

follow_ups.question: What tools do you use most?
follow_ups.response: Excel, Power BI, SAP, NetSuite, Tableau sometimes, and a lot of PowerPoint for executive communication.

follow_ups.question: Do you supervise people?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I directly mentor and manage junior analysts and coordinate with managers in other departments.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep a pretty structured personal finance routine because that is how my brain works. Sunday evenings I review spending, update savings goals, and plan meals. I also water my vegetable garden, prep lunches, and check my calendar for workouts and volunteer commitments. I teach financial-literacy sessions at community centers a few times a quarter, usually on budgeting, credit, or basic investing.

follow_ups.question: What do you grow in your garden?
follow_ups.response: Tomatoes, basil, peppers, herbs, and sometimes cucumbers if the heat does not ruin them.

follow_ups.question: How much time does volunteering take?
follow_ups.response: Maybe four to six hours in a typical month, more if I am preparing a new workshop.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is that I have been studying more seriously for the CPA path and exploring CFA materials. That means fewer spontaneous weeknight plans and more scheduled study blocks. I also added a regular Wednesday yoga class because I noticed my stress was getting too physical: tight shoulders, shallow sleep, too much laptop time. At work, AI-enabled analytics pilots have added learning time to my week.

follow_ups.question: When do you study?
follow_ups.response: Mostly 7:30 to 9:00 on weeknights and a longer block on Sunday afternoon.

follow_ups.question: What did you give up to make room?
follow_ups.response: Some TV, some casual scrolling, and a few social plans during budget season.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine for kids. My weekday routine is centered around work, exercise, studying, and community commitments.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with nieces, nephews, or younger relatives?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. I will help family when needed, but I am not part of a daily childcare routine.

follow_ups.question: Does not having children affect your schedule?
follow_ups.response: It gives me more flexibility for work travel, evening events, and study time.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My direct experiences have been limited. I have had a couple of traffic stops, one for a brake light and one for speeding years ago, and both were routine. I have interacted with police at community events and road closures. I do think about policing more broadly because friends and neighbors have had different experiences depending on race, age, and where they were stopped.

follow_ups.question: How did those traffic stops feel?
follow_ups.response: Nerve-racking, even though they were routine. I kept my hands visible and tried to be very calm.

follow_ups.question: Do you know local officers personally?
follow_ups.response: Not personally, only through community events or neighborhood safety meetings.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A neighborhood car break-in situation stands out. Police took reports, but most of the actual prevention came from neighbors sharing camera footage and reminders.

follow_ups.question: Was your car affected?
follow_ups.response: No, but several cars in the community were.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became more consistent about locking the car and not leaving anything visible.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has been arrested. I know acquaintances who have dealt with DUI or minor legal trouble, but not close family.

follow_ups.question: Has that shaped your views?
follow_ups.response: It means my personal experience is limited, so I try to listen when others describe more serious encounters.

follow_ups.question: Any legal system involvement otherwise?
follow_ups.response: Only ordinary things like jury summons and traffic citations.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, including presidential, midterm, and local elections. I missed one small municipal runoff years ago and felt annoyed with myself afterward. In Georgia, voting feels consequential, so I pay attention to registration deadlines, early voting locations, and ballot questions. I also remind friends to check their registration, though I try not to be pushy.

follow_ups.question: How do you usually vote?
follow_ups.response: Usually early in person, because it fits my schedule and reduces election-day uncertainty.

follow_ups.question: What races do you research most?
follow_ups.response: Local school board, county commission, judges, and statewide offices.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as center-left, pragmatic, and institutionally minded. I usually vote Democratic, but I am not someone who treats party labels as a substitute for competence. Economic opportunity, education, voting access, health care affordability, climate risk, and corporate accountability matter to me. Because I work in finance, I care about fiscal discipline and whether programs can actually be administered well, but I do not think fiscal responsibility means ignoring inequality. I support ESG reporting and transparency, though I think it has to be measurable and not just branding. On social issues, I am generally progressive: I support reproductive rights, LGBTQ rights, and racial equity. My politics are shaped by growing up in diverse Gwinnett, working in corporate settings, and volunteering with people who are trying to get financially stable.

follow_ups.question: What does pragmatic mean to you politically?
follow_ups.response: It means I want values plus execution. A policy can sound good and still fail if the systems, funding, or data are weak.

follow_ups.question: Are there issues where you are more moderate?
follow_ups.response: I am cautious about broad promises without funding plans, and I think small businesses need to be considered when regulations change.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on local politics and implementation. Earlier, I cared mostly about national elections and big issues. Now I see how zoning, transit, school funding, tax administration, and county services shape daily life. I have also become more concerned about misinformation because I see smart people share bad data if it confirms what they already feel.

follow_ups.question: What changed that focus?
follow_ups.response: Living as a homeowner and volunteering locally made county decisions feel very concrete.

follow_ups.question: Have your party preferences changed?
follow_ups.response: Not dramatically. I am still closer to Democrats, but I am more attentive to local competence.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot, especially after 2020. I would not say I was unaware before, but the national attention forced me to examine what I had treated as background noise. In Gwinnett, you can live around diversity and still miss unequal experiences if you are not listening closely. Friends shared stories about traffic stops, workplace assumptions, and school discipline that made the issue feel personal and local.

follow_ups.question: Did it change any behavior for you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became more intentional about reading local reporting, donating to legal aid groups, and discussing equity at work.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one peaceful march in Atlanta in 2020 with friends, but most of my response has been conversations and civic engagement.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as questions of accountability, dignity, and systems. It is not only individual prejudice; it is also data, incentives, training, oversight, and whose complaints get taken seriously. My finance brain goes to measurement: stops, use-of-force patterns, complaint resolution, funding priorities. But my human reaction is simpler: people should not have to calculate whether a routine encounter will become dangerous.

follow_ups.question: Do people at work discuss this?
follow_ups.response: Some do, especially in DEI settings, but people are careful. I try to keep it practical and respectful.

follow_ups.question: What reforms do you support?
follow_ups.response: Better data transparency, independent review, de-escalation training, and more mental-health crisis response options.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race in the U.S. is both deeply historical and very present. In my own life, I move through a multicultural community and feel proud of that, but I also see unequal wealth, school access, housing patterns, and health outcomes. My Hispanic surname sometimes opens conversations about identity, but I am also aware that my experience is not the same as friends who are Black or visibly immigrant. I try to stay humble and specific rather than turning race into slogans.

follow_ups.question: How does your own background shape that?
follow_ups.response: It makes me comfortable with mixed identity, but it also reminds me that cultural diversity alone does not solve structural inequality.

follow_ups.question: Where do you learn about these issues?
follow_ups.response: Local journalism, books, podcasts, workplace panels, and direct conversations with friends.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and friends, joined one protest, donated modestly, and tried to support equity work in my workplace. I am not a public activist every week, but I do not keep it entirely private either.

follow_ups.question: Were those family conversations hard?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. People agree on fairness in the abstract but differ on what accountability should look like.

follow_ups.question: What workplace action did you take?
follow_ups.response: I helped review mentorship access and recruiting metrics for finance roles.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My close friends are mostly concerned and engaged, though in different ways. Some marched, some donated, some focused on school equity or workplace DEI. My parents are sympathetic but more cautious in how they talk about policing because they grew up with a stronger instinct to trust institutions. My brother is probably the most direct in calling out racial bias when he sees it.

follow_ups.question: Has it caused conflict?
follow_ups.response: A little tension, but not lasting conflict. We usually come back to wanting people treated fairly.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends discuss politics often?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but usually over dinner or texts, not as the only thing we talk about.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall my health is good. I am active, I do yoga, run 5Ks, hike on weekends, and cook most of my meals. I do carry work stress in my body, especially neck and shoulder tension, and I have had mild anxiety during high-pressure periods. I do not have a major chronic illness. I try to be preventive with annual checkups, dental visits, vaccines, and sleep routines.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually four or five times a week, mixing yoga, walking, running, and hikes.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest to maintain?
follow_ups.response: Sleep during budget season. I can be disciplined all day and still answer emails too late.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because I know how to plan, cook, and schedule exercise. It is harder when work deadlines compress everything and I spend too many hours sitting. Travel and late meetings can throw off meals and sleep.

follow_ups.question: What foods help you stay on track?
follow_ups.response: Salmon, vegetables, rice bowls, soups, yogurt, fruit, and big Sunday meal prep.

follow_ups.question: What throws you off?
follow_ups.response: Back-to-back meetings, airport food, and stress snacking on crackers or chocolate.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge medically. I had a mild ankle sprain after a trail hike last year and had to pause running for a few weeks. I also started paying more attention to stress-related headaches and shoulder tension, which led me to commit to regular yoga and ergonomic changes at my desk. No major diagnosis, surgery, or hospitalization.

follow_ups.question: Did you get treatment for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: I went to urgent care, got it checked, rested, iced it, and did basic physical therapy exercises.

follow_ups.question: Have the headaches improved?
follow_ups.response: Yes, when I keep up yoga, hydration, and screen breaks.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously interfered with work. Stress can reduce my patience or sleep, but I have not had to stop working because of it.

follow_ups.question: Do you take sick days?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but rarely. I am trying to be better about not working through everything.

follow_ups.question: Any caregiving impact with children?
follow_ups.response: No, I do not have children.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, in a moderate way. My dad manages high blood pressure, and my mom has had some knee pain that limits long walks. I help by going to appointments when needed, translating insurance or billing details, and nudging them toward preventive care. It is not full-time caregiving, but it is part of my mental checklist.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help with appointments?
follow_ups.response: A few times a year, mainly if there is a specialist or billing issue.

follow_ups.question: Does it worry you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly because I can see them aging and I want them to stay independent.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I am fortunate to have employer health insurance, so I have not had to forgo necessary care. The frustrating parts are scheduling, prior authorizations, and deciphering bills. For my parents, I sometimes help compare providers or read explanation-of-benefits statements. Access is manageable for us, but only because we have insurance, cars, and enough financial cushion.

follow_ups.question: What care is hardest to schedule?
follow_ups.response: Specialists and physical therapy appointments at convenient times.

follow_ups.question: Have costs surprised you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, imaging and lab bills can be surprisingly opaque even with insurance.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing extreme, but yes in everyday ways. I use yoga, meditation, herbal teas, massage, and occasional acupuncture for stress and muscle tension. My family has home remedies like ginger tea, honey, soups, and stretching before jumping to medication for minor things. But for serious issues, we use regular medical care.

follow_ups.question: How often do you use acupuncture?
follow_ups.response: Only a few times a year, usually when my shoulders are really tight.

follow_ups.question: Do you see it as spiritual or physical?
follow_ups.response: Mostly physical and stress-related, though yoga has a reflective side for me.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, maybe wine with dinner or a cocktail at a concert, but not as my main coping tool. During tough times I am more likely to overwork, clean the kitchen, bake bread, go to yoga, or do a crossword. If I drink when stressed, I keep it to one glass because I know it affects my sleep.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink in a typical week?
follow_ups.response: Usually one or two drinks total, sometimes none.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever smoked?
follow_ups.response: No, not beyond maybe trying a puff once in college.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other recreational drugs. I use ordinary over-the-counter medication like ibuprofen for headaches or soreness. I am not on anxiety medication or pain medication. The most recent example was taking ibuprofen after a long hike because my ankle felt tender.

follow_ups.question: Any prescription medications?
follow_ups.response: No regular prescriptions right now.

follow_ups.question: Why avoid marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Mostly personal preference and job caution. I do not like feeling foggy.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I pay through employer insurance, an HSA, and regular budgeting for copays and prescriptions. My parents have insurance as well, and they can cover their care, though I help them understand bills. I keep a health line item in my budget because surprise medical expenses are not really surprising anymore.

follow_ups.question: Do you contribute to an HSA?
follow_ups.response: Yes, every paycheck, and I try not to spend it unless needed.

follow_ups.question: Any unpaid medical debt?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccine. I get recommended vaccines, including flu and COVID boosters when advised, because I see them as basic prevention.

follow_ups.question: Did your family feel the same?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes. My parents had questions early on, but they got vaccinated.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad worked as a logistics operations supervisor. He coordinated shipments, managed schedules, supervised warehouse or distribution staff, solved delivery problems, and kept operations moving on time.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes early mornings or late days when shipments had issues.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from him?
follow_ups.response: Reliability, planning, and staying calm when something goes wrong.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for a regional distribution and logistics company. They moved consumer goods and business supplies through warehouses and delivery routes around the Southeast.

follow_ups.question: Was it corporate or small business?
follow_ups.response: A mid-sized company with corporate systems but local operations.

follow_ups.question: Did his job influence your finance interest?
follow_ups.response: Indirectly, yes. I saw how operations, timing, and costs connect.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: In a few years I hope to be a Director of Finance, with a team that is strong, ethical, and genuinely useful to the business. I want to have made real progress on CPA and CFA credentials, and I want to lead larger projects like M&A due diligence, ESG reporting, and digital finance transformation. Personally, I hope I am still close to my family and friends, still cooking, hiking, doing yoga, and not letting ambition flatten my life. I would love to travel to Kyoto during cherry blossom season and to the Canadian Rockies. Longer term, I want to build a nonprofit financial-literacy program in Gwinnett County, especially for women, young adults, and underserved communities. I also hope for partnership someday, but I do not want to build my identity around waiting for it.

follow_ups.question: What would success feel like day to day?
follow_ups.response: Calm competence: meaningful work, healthy routines, time for people, and fewer nights answering emails at 10:30.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward the nonprofit idea?
follow_ups.response: Piloting a workshop series with community centers and measuring what participants actually need.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value integrity, growth, family, community, and steadiness. Integrity matters because money and power can distort decisions if people are not grounded. Growth matters because I do not want to coast. Family and community matter because achievement feels empty if it is only individual. And steadiness matters because I want to be the person people can count on in a stressful room.

follow_ups.question: Where do you see those values most clearly?
follow_ups.response: In mentoring analysts, showing up for family, and teaching financial-literacy classes.

follow_ups.question: What value is hardest to live consistently?
follow_ups.response: Balance. I believe in it, but ambition can crowd it out.
